title: Why do prices rise even when a product stays the same?
sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index

lines.text: Why did a McDonald's hamburger cost fifteen cents in the nineteen-fifties, but costs several dollars today?
lines.caps: Why does everything get *more | expensive over *time?

lines.text: The burger didn't get ten times bigger or more delicious; the value of your dollar shrank.
lines.caps: The product didn't change; your *dollar | lost purchasing *power!

lines.text: This steady price increase is called inflation, and it happens when money supply outpaces real goods.
lines.caps: Inflation occurs when *money supply | outpaces available *goods

lines.text: When central banks expand money and credit, more dollars compete for the same supply of eggs, oil, and homes.
lines.caps: More dollars *competing | for the exact same *goods

lines.text: Producers face rising wages and shipping costs, passing those expenses directly to grocery shelf price tags.
lines.caps: Producers pass higher *costs | directly to consumer *shelves

lines.text: A healthy economy targets two percent annual inflation to encourage people to invest and spend rather than hoard cash.
To beat inflation, always invest your savings in assets that grow faster than the money supply.
lines.caps: Invest your money to *beat | inflation's silent *tax!
